lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- Flagging the Problem
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Paula Teodoro Valdivia | Lesson 1 -- Flagging the Problem
lesson.grammar_point: modals of obligation and recommendation (must / have to / should)

listenings.text: I run global contracts for a group with operations in eleven countries, and I sit in about six of these review calls every week. Let me tell you what I actually need from local counsel, because most lawyers get this wrong. I do not need the full analysis read out loud. I have the document. What I need, in the first thirty seconds, is one sentence: which clause is the problem, and how bad is it. Then I need to know what you recommend. Not five options. One recommendation, with the reason behind it. The lawyers I trust the most are not the ones with perfect English. They are the ones who tell me straight away that clause fourteen is unenforceable in their country, that it exposes us to a fine, and that we should replace it with standard local wording. That is a thirty second answer and it saves me a week. If your English is not perfect, I honestly do not care. Just lead with the problem.

For a long time I prepared for these calls in the wrong way. I read the whole contract again the night before, I translated my notes word by word, and then I arrived at the meeting with four pages and no idea where to start. And of course I froze. What changed everything was a very small habit. Now, before every call, I write three lines and only three. The first line says which clause worries me. The second line says what happens if nobody touches it. The third line says what I want them to do about it. Three lines. That is my whole script. The strange part is that my English did not improve overnight, but people started saying that I was clearer than before. I was not clearer in English. I was clearer in my head, and the English simply followed.

extra_audio.text: My main concern is clause fourteen, the indemnity. As it is written, there is no cap, so our liability is unlimited. We should cap it at the annual contract value. It is a short amendment, not a new contract.
